newsitem.title: USA: SOCCER-CONCACAF TO BATTLE BOGUS TICKETS AFTER STADIUM TRAGEDY.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-CONCACAF TO BATTLE BOGUS TICKETS AFTER STADIUM TRAGEDY.

text.p: CONCACAF officials on Wednesday promised an effort to halt sales of counterfeit ticktes, which they believe contributed to scores of deaths at at a Guatamala World Cup soccer qualifier last week.
CONCACAF President Jack Warner announced the formation of a Special Commission to study and make recommendations regarding the problem of counterfeit tickets for official events.

"In light of the tremendous tragedy of last week in Guatemala, and the apparent relationship of counterfeit tickets, it is incumbent upon us to take action to protect the public from this type of criminal behaviour," Warner said.
Last Wednesday, 81 people were killed in an avalanche of bodies at Mateo Flores Stadium in Guatemala City prior to a CONCACAF zone World Cup qualifying match between Guatemala and Costa Rica.

Many of the victims were crushed against fences separating the pitch from the seats and the use of fences has been widely criticised by international soccer officials. But tremendous overcrowding in the stadium has been blamed on lax security and sale of counterfeit tickets.
"Counterfeiting has always been a problem, but until now has only had financial consequences," CONCACAF General Secretary Chuck Blazer said.
"We must effectively put an end to this dangerous and criminal behaviour, now responsible for the loss of life. It cannot be tolerated."
Toward that end, Warner appointed Blazer to chair the six person Special Commission dedicated to developing "a policy which can move towards eliminating counterfeit tickets as a destructive scourge."
The Commission will hold its first meeting at the Confederation's New York offices on November 1, Warner said.
With World Cup Qualifying matches continuing through the end of 1997, Blazer said: "We recognise the urgency of this task. We will not fail.
"Radical measures may have to be taken. The public demands and has the right to expect that we assure their safety."
